en: Chapter One: The Gate of Skillful Means of Non-arising in the Mahāyāna, which generally reveals the essence of the Buddha-body. Chapter Two: Opening the Door of Wisdom. Chapter Three:
Manifesting the Inconceivable Dharma. Chapter Four: Clarifying the True Nature of All Dharmas. Chapter Five: Natural Unimpeded Understanding.
The Path of Liberation: Each person should kneel with palms joined and be instructed to make the Four Great Vows: "Sentient beings are boundless; I vow to deliver them all.
Afflictions are boundless; I vow to sever them all."

"I vow to study the inexhaustible Dharma gates; I vow to realize the unsurpassed Buddha-way. Next, request the Buddhas of the ten directions to serve as preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and so forth. Next, request the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time. Next, instruct them in the reception of the Three Refuges. Next, inquire regarding the five capabilities: 1. Are you able, from this day until reaching *bodhi*, to abandon all evil associates? Or are you unable? 2. Are you able to draw near to virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*)? Or are you unable? 3. Are you able to sit and maintain the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*) until the end of your life without violating them? Or are you unable? 4. Are you able to read and recite Mahāyāna sūtras and inquire into their profound meanings? Or are you unable? 5. Are you able to protect and rescue suffering sentient beings according to your strength? Or are you unable? Next, each shall state their own name and repent of their transgressions, saying: "I repent of the ten non-virtuous sins of body, speech, and mind committed in the past, future, and present lives."
I now repent with a sincere heart;

may my transgressions be extinguished so that they never arise again. As for the grave offenses of the five heinous crimes and other heavy karmic hindrances, let them be dealt with as previously described: it is like a bright pearl submerged in turbid water, which becomes clear immediately through the power of the pearl.
The purifying power of the Buddha-nature is likewise;
the turbid waters of affliction are all rendered pure.
You have completed your repentance, and the three karmas are now purified.
Like pure lapis lazuli, transparent both inside and out,
he is fit to receive the pure Bodhisattva precepts;
this is the upholding of the mental precepts.
Taking buddha-nature as the precept:
if a thought arises even momentarily within one's nature, it immediately violates buddha-nature;
this is the breaking of the bodhisattva precepts.
To protect the mind so that it does not arise is to accord with the Buddha-nature.

This is the upholding of the Bodhisattva precepts. After the three recitations, have each person sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). To have the mind of a Buddha-son (*jinaputra*) tranquil and unmoving is called "submergence" (*nimajjana*). It is said to be "pure. O Buddha-sons, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess a great skillful means for entering the Way.
With a single thought of pure mind, one suddenly transcends to the stage of Buddhahood. Chant "Namo Amitābha Buddha" in unison while striking the wooden clapper.
The chant says: "All marks must not be grasped," as stated in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
All phenomena that possess marks are entirely illusory.
If the mind is observed and becomes pure, it is called the "Pure Ground of Mind.
Do not contract the body and mind; rather, expand and relax the body and mind.
He looked out expansively and distantly, viewing all things with equanimity as far as the limits of space.
Huo asked him, "What do you see? The disciple said, "I do not see a single thing. Huo [replied].
"Look pure; look minutely.
This means to use the pure eye of mind, boundless and limitless, setting aside distant gazing. [The Master] speaks in harmony.
He asks: "Look without obstruction. [The student] speaks in harmony. He asks: "What do you see? [The student] answers.
Without seeing a single thing, look far ahead;
look far behind; look simultaneously and with equal clarity toward the four intermediate directions, above, and below.
Gaze throughout the entirety of empty space.
Always gaze with the eye of the pure mind;
do not allow for interruption, nor limit the extent of your gazing.
To "cause them to attain" means that body and mind are harmoniously employed without obstruction.
Regarding the phrase "three sixes," the disciple said: "This refers to the Buddha’s body and mind being free from discursive thought."
Not seeing the mind as mind, one attains liberation through the mind;
not seeing the body as form, one is liberated through the body.
Thus, for a long time without interruption, one enters by means of speech [realizing] that space is devoid of even a single thing.
Pure and devoid of marks,
one should always maintain this without interruption;
from this, one will forever be free from hindrances.
The eye faculty is pure;
the eye faculty is free from hindrances.
The ear faculty is pure.
The ear is free from the obstructions of the sense-faculties;
in this manner, up to the six faculties, they are purified and free from obstructions.
That all things are without obstruction is itself liberation.
One does not perceive the characteristics of the six sense faculties;
they are pure and devoid of marks.
That which is constant and uninterrupted is itself the Buddha.
This is what it means to be the Buddha.
The Buddha-mind is pure, transcending both existence and non-existence.

When body and mind do not arise, one constantly maintains the true mind; this is what is meant by "submergence" (immersion) into True Suchness (*tathatā*). When the mind does not give rise to [discursive] mind, that is the True Suchness of the mind.
Form does not arise from the suchness of form;
because of the suchness of mind, the mind is liberated;
because of the suchness of form, form is liberated.
When both mind and form are detached, there is not even a single thing;
this is the Great Bodhi Tree. "Buddha" is a Sanskrit term from the Western regions;
here in this land, it is translated as "Awakening" (Jue).
That which is called awakening is the essence of the mind, free from thought.
As for the characteristic of being free from thought,
it is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception.
The single characteristic of the dharma-realm is the Tathāgata’s equal dharma-body;
this dharma-body is designated as "original enlightenment" (mūla-awakening).
When the awakened mind first arises, the mind has no initial characteristic.
Far removed from even subtle thoughts,
one clearly perceives the nature of the mind;
this abiding nature is called ultimate awakening.
"Buddha" is a term from the Sanskrit language of the Western Regions;
here it is translated as "Awakening.
As for the meaning of "awakening," it refers to the essence of the mind being free from thought; this freedom from thought is the meaning of "Buddha" and the meaning of "Awakening."
A brief explanation of the meaning of "Buddha" (Buddha):
it fully encompasses three meanings and is also called the "Convenient Means for Sealing the Mind.
Question: What are these three meanings?
Self-awakening, awakening others, and the fulfillment of awakening are free from the mind.
Self-awakening does not depend on the five sense organs;
it is free from form in awakening others.
Not conditioned by the five sensory objects,
with both mind and form detached, awakening and practice are perfected;
this is the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body.
That which is free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception. Question:
In what way is it equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception?
Question: Is this cessation universal or non-universal? Answer:
Space is without mind; it is free from thought and without mind.
When there is no mind, it is equal to empty space, pervading everywhere;
when there is thought, it does not pervade;
when free from thought, it pervades.
The single characteristic of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is the Tathāgata’s equal dharma-body (dharmakāya). Question:
What is this dharma-realm? It is known by the mind as being the Dharma.
The "elements" (dhātu) refer to the eighteen elements.
When the eye sees and the mind cognizes, many thoughts arise, giving rise to obstructions and barriers that prevent penetration.
These are the defiled dharmadhātu; these are the sentient-being realm (sattvadhātu).
This is the cessation; this is the pure dharma-realm.
When seen by the eye and known by the mind, it is free from conceptual thought and thus devoid of obstruction.
This pure dharma-realm is the Buddha-realm.
This extinction is the Buddha-realm;
it is the single characteristic of the Dharma-realm, the sphere known by the mind.
This dharma is the Dharma-realm.
The eye sees forms;
the ear hears sounds;
the nose perceives fragrances.
The tongue cognizes tastes;
the body perceives tangibles;
the mind cognizes mental phenomena.
One should understand that the aforementioned five kinds of dharmas,
when the mind arises with a common object,
are themselves the defiled dharma-realm and the realm of sentient beings.
If one does not give rise to the thought of commonality with objects,
then the pure dharma-realm is itself the Buddha-realm;
the dharma-realm is of a single characteristic.
Within the eighteen elements (dhātus), there are two types:
one is defiled and the other is pure;
first defiled, then pure.
The eye sees forms;
the mental consciousness cognizes them by sharing the same object.
The five faculties, such as the eye, depend upon their respective objects.
The arising of defilement in five locations is the defilement of all locations; the defilement of all locations is the dharma-realm of defilement, which is the realm of sentient beings. Question:
What is this "submergence"? What is this "contention" regarding the dharma-realm?
Regarding the pure dharma-realm:
within the state free from conceptual thought, one sees forms with the eye without discrimination;
thus, one attains liberation within the very locus of the eye.
The same applies to the other four.
Regarding the fivefold liberation and the universal liberation:
universal liberation is itself the purity of all places.
This is precisely the pure dharma-realm, which is the Buddha-realm.
For those who are free from the marks of conceptual thought,
it is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception.
Belonging to one’s own dharma-realm is identical to belonging to others. Question:
What is the meaning of "this is the Tathāgata"? Answer:
It is the mind that is free from the mind.
The suchness of form apart from form;
the suchness of both mind and form—
this is the fulfillment of awakening.
The fulfillment of awakening is itself the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, when the mental faculty does not arise, it is the suchness of mind;
when the five faculties do not arise, they are the suchness of form.
When the mind and form are suchness (*tathatā*) and do not arise in accordance with objects,
this is precisely the Tathāgata’s equal *dharmakāya*.
This *dharmakāya* is designated as "original enlightenment" (*mūla-awakening*).
When the mind first arises in awakening, the mind has no initial characteristic.
Being far removed from subtle thoughts, one clearly perceives the nature of the mind;
this eternally abiding nature is called the ultimate.
This is the Dharma-body. Question:
Is this the Reward-body Buddha?
It is known that the six roots are fundamentally unmoving, the awakened nature is suddenly perfected, and its luminosity shines everywhere.
This is the reward-body Buddha (saṃbhogakāya). This is the dharma-body Buddha (dharmakāya), which is that which has entered [nirvāṇa].
It is because of having cultivated precepts, concentration, and wisdom during the causal stage.
Having shattered the thick, layered obstructions of ignorance within the body,
one achieves the great radiance of wisdom;
this is the Dharmakāya Buddha.
This is the Nirmanakaya Buddha;
it is as when the mind is free from discursive thought and the sensory objects are purified,
such that knowledge and vision are unimpeded.
Pervading the ten directions in perfect response,
this is the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha;
its essence and function are clearly distinct.
Freedom from thought is called the essence;
seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are its functions.
It is quiescent yet constantly active.
Functioning while constantly quiescent:
thus, function is itself quiescence.
To be free from characteristics is called quiescence.
Quiescence-illumination and illumination-quiescence.
As for quiescence-illumination:
it is the arising of characteristics from the nature.
As for "illumination within stillness": when gathered, its characteristics are subsumed within its fundamental nature;
when extended, it pervades the entire dharma-realm.
When rolled up, it is entirely contained within the tip of a hair;
when exhaled and inhaled, its divine function is distinct and sovereign. When one examines the body and mind, they are already empty—who exhales and who inhales?
Since body and mind are empty, there is no exhaling or inhaling.
This is to unite with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
To open to the unconditioned is to penetrate the true mark (*dharmatā*).
With body and mind empty, one skillfully dedicates [the merit].
Dedicate [merit] toward Bodhi to realize the true, eternal bliss.
Constantly facing sensory objects, the mind remains unattached.
Regarding the two phenomena of body and mind, they are both defiled and pure.
Based on the presence of mindfulness, there are immeasurable, Ganges-sand-like afflictions;
based on the absence of mindfulness, there are immeasurable, Ganges-sand-like merits.
Based on these immeasurable, Ganges-sand-like merits, it is pure.
That which is based upon this is the dharma-body;
that which perishes is the body based upon the mind.
Freedom from conceptualization is the dharma-body.
Because of being free from discursive thought, one transforms immeasurable, Ganges-sand-like instances of arising and ceasing into immeasurable, Ganges-sand-like merits;
these Ganges-sand-like merits have this dwelling in freedom from discursive thought as their basis.
This refers to the meaning of "extinction" and "accumulation.
Uninterrupted practice that sustains meritorious qualities so they do not disperse is "accumulation.
By accumulating these various merits, one fills the Dharmakāya.
Because one is free from thought, the myriad objects are all true. [End of] the first section. Second: The Preceptor struck the wooden block and asked, "Do you hear the sound?
"I hear it. "When you hear it, do you move? "I do not move. This is non-movement.
This is the skillful means of generating wisdom from meditative concentration;
it is the opening of the door to wisdom.
Upon hearing this wisdom, [one attains it].
This skillful means is not only able to give rise to wisdom,
but can also bring about right concentration;
it is the gateway that opens the door to knowledge.
One immediately attains wisdom;
this is called opening the gate of wisdom.
If one does not obtain these skillful means, [one cannot do so].
Rightness immediately falls into false concentration;
by greedily clinging to the flavor of dhyāna, one falls into the two vehicles.
Having already attained this skillful means of right concentration, one enters nirvāṇa.
To immediately attain parinirvāṇa is the Great Nirvana.
The functioning of wisdom is the application of insight.
This is called opening up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Knowledge and vision are themselves bodhi. Question: What is this "immovability"? Answer: The immovability of the mind—this immovability of the mind is concentration, it is wisdom, and it is principle.
The immovability of the faculty of hearing—this is form, it is phenomena, and it is discernment.
This immovability is the skillful means of generating wisdom from meditative concentration;
it opens the gate of wisdom. Question:
What is this gate of wisdom?
The faculty of hearing is the gateway to wisdom.
By practicing non-arising and non-perishing, one opens the gateway to wisdom;
when hearing sounds, the faculty of hearing remains unmoved.
This is the opening of the gate of wisdom;
this is the immersion in wisdom, and this is the hearing of wisdom.
The five faculties are, in their entirety, the gate of wisdom.
It not only gives rise to wisdom but also brings about right concentration;
it is the gateway to knowledge. Question:
What is this gateway to knowledge?
The faculty of mind is the gateway to wisdom.
It acts as the gateway to wisdom for the opening of death and birth.
The immovability of the faculty of mind is the opening of the gateway to wisdom.
When one forms the intention to effect the transition from death to birth, wisdom is immediately attained;
this is called "opening the gate of wisdom.
I have now finished opening the gate of wisdom for you.
There are sentient beings possessed of power whose bodies, hands, and feet remain tranquil, peaceful, and unmoving;
they cannot be shaken by the eight winds. Question: [Why is this so?]
These are the eight winds that cause one to sink.
As for the eight winds— gain and loss, defamation and praise, fame and insignificance, suffering and pleasure—
the answer is that four of them are adverse.
Question: Regarding these four cases of conformity and opposition, what occurs at the point of death and rebirth? Answer:
The mind remains unmoving.
Immovability is the Buddha.
Like Mount Sumeru, he stands far beyond the ocean of birth and death;
he dwells in leisure, having transcended the three realms.
Adorned by the power of the Dharma, concentration, and wisdom as they have been attained,
he delivers sentient beings and personally realizes the unsurpassed path. Question:
"How many kinds of people can open the gate of wisdom? Answer:
"There are three kinds of people:
ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas."
Ordinary beings hear when there is sound and do not hear when there is no sound; once the sound has subsided, they do not hear it.
Those of the Two Vehicles [hear] both when there is sound and when there is no sound.
When sound falls away, it is no longer heard.
Whether the Bodhisattva has sound or is without sound, it is not heard.
The sound has fallen away, yet it is heard constantly. Question:
These three people have opened the same single gate of wisdom;
for what reason have they passed away?
Those of the two vehicles, being greedily attached to the flavor of dhyāna, fall into the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles.
Those of the two vehicles open but a single gate of wisdom;
this wisdom is the wisdom of hearing realized through the faculty of the ear.
What was previously unheard has now been heard;
having heard it, joy arises in the mind,
and through that joy, the body is moved.
Fearing movement, one clings to immobility;
by extinguishing the six consciousnesses, one realizes emptiness and stillness.
Nirvana exists whether there is sound or no sound.
When the sound falls away and ceases to be heard,
one does not hear it; thus, through attachment to the flavor of dhyāna,
one falls into the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles.
The Bodhisattva opens the gate of wisdom;
hearing this wisdom at the faculty of the ear, they realize the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
They know that the six sense bases are fundamentally unmoving, whether sound exists or does not exist.
When sounds fall away,
one constantly hears and constantly accords with the immovable practice.
By attaining this skillful means of right concentration, one immediately attains parinirvāṇa, which is the Great Nirvana.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Not hearing what is heard, not hearing what is not heard, hearing what is not heard, and hearing what is heard. Question:
What is this "not hearing what is heard"?
"That which was not heard before is now heard;
this is 'hearing what was not heard. This is submerged, yet it is 'not heard.
Having heard what was not heard, joy arises in the mind."
Joy immediately moves;
fearing movement, one clings to non-movement.
By extinguishing the six consciousnesses, one realizes emptiness and stillness.
Nirvana has both sound and no-sound.
When sound falls away and is not heard, that non-hearing is itself non-hearing.
This is cessation; this is hearing.
Once joy has arisen in the mind,
that joy immediately causes movement;
fearing this movement, one clings to immobility.
When the six consciousnesses are extinguished and one realizes the emptiness and stillness of nirvāṇa, there may be sound or no sound.
When the sound falls away, it is not heard; this "not hearing" is neither hearing nor non-hearing.
This is both submerged and the non-hearing of what was heard.
When those of the two vehicles emerge from meditative concentration,
they hear what was not heard while in concentration;
this is because those of the two vehicles lack wisdom while in concentration.
They are unable to preach the Dharma, nor can they deliver sentient beings.
Upon emerging from meditative concentration, their minds are distracted; when preaching the Dharma, they lack stability.
Moisture and wetness are called "dry wisdom.
Concentration is either heard or not heard;
it is either submerged or heard. Even ordinary people hear what is heard.
It is said that Bodhisattvas also have hearing.

When ordinary beings hear, their hearing is stirred; being stirred, they become one with the dust of the world. When Bodhisattvas hear, their hearing is not stirred, and thus they do not become one with the dust.
They harmonize with the light of the world yet remain untainted by it. In the Sahā world, Śākyamuni Tathāgata performs the Buddha-work through sound.
The faculty of the ear is a gateway to wisdom.
In the world of Radiance, the Tathāgata Lamp-Light performs the Buddha-work through light.
The faculty of the eye is a gateway to wisdom.
In the world of Gandhavatī, the Tathāgata Gandhottama performs the Buddha-work through various fragrances;
the faculty of the nose serves as the gateway to wisdom.
In the world of Amṛta, the Tathāgata Amṛtābha performs the Buddha-work through the taste of ambrosia.
The tongue faculty is a gateway to wisdom.
In the world of *Puṣpa*, the Tathāgata Puṣpaprabha performs buddha-work by means of various flowers. The body faculty is a gateway to wisdom.
In the world of *Suvijñapti*, the Tathāgata Dharmaprabhāsa performs buddha-work by knowing all phenomena as immovable.
The faculty of mind (*manas*) is the gateway to wisdom (*prajñā*).
This skillful means (*upāya*) is not only able to give rise to wisdom, but is also capable of right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*). Question:
Is this a state of being lost, or is it wrong concentration (*mithyāsamādhi*) or right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*)?
Those of the two vehicles extinguish the six consciousnesses to realize the emptiness and stillness of nirvana;
this is a state of false certainty. Bodhisattvas know that the six roots are fundamentally unmoving, whether sound exists or not.
The sound falls away, yet there is constant hearing;
this is right concentration. Question:
Who is able to open the gate of wisdom?
A virtuous friend can open [this realization].
By hearing the words of a virtuous friend, one awakens to the fact that the six sense-faculties are fundamentally unmoving; whether there is sound or no sound, the sound falls away and vanishes.
Constantly hearing, constantly complying with, and practicing without wavering—this is called the external spiritual friend who can open the gate of wisdom. Question:
What is the internal spiritual friend? Answer:
Wisdom is the knowledge that "this is knowledge" and "this is discernment. When the mind is transformed into wisdom, it opens the gate of wisdom.
Attaining this very wisdom is called having an internal spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), which is able to open the gate of wisdom.
This refers to those who have fallen away and those who are fixed in either the wrong or the right determination.
For persons of the two vehicles, having concentration but lacking wisdom is called "wrong";
for Bodhisattvas, having both concentration and wisdom is called "right. Question:
This "extinction" (nirodha) refers to the Great and Small Nirvāṇas.
In the Western land [of India], it is a Sanskrit term;
here in this land [of China], it has been translated as "perfect quiescence" (yuánjì).
"Extinction" (nirodha) and "parinirvāṇa" refer to the simultaneous stilling of both [afflictions and] wisdom; this is Great Nirvana. "Bodhi" is a Sanskrit term from the Western regions;
here, it is translated as "knowledge.
Knowledge is seeing, and seeing is the function of stilling wisdom.
Bodhi is the quiescent function of nirvāṇa;
knowledge and vision are its function,
and wisdom is its essence.

Bodhi is the function; Nirvana is the essence. When essence and function are clearly distinguished, the Sūtra says: "Nirvana cannot be attained through mind or body. It also says: "Bodhi cannot be attained through mind or body. It further states: "The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is neither form nor mind. It also says: "The Buddha has no body, yet he manifests bodies; he has no mind, yet he manifests minds. It also says: "The Buddha’s body is not born from parents. This bodhi is the cessation of all marks. Question:

The mind is unmoving, free from thought, and does not arise.
Awakening cannot be attained by means of the mind;
since form is unmoving, free from thought, and unarisen, awakening cannot be attained by means of the body.
When both body and mind are unmoving, that is quiescent extinction.
This bodhi is so called because it extinguishes all marks.
Furthermore, when both body and mind are free from discursive thought, that is the perfection of bodhi. Question:
Awakening is not something that can be attained,

Answer: When the six sense faculties are unmoving and do not encounter the various sense bases,

Furthermore, when the faculties and their objects are undefiled, there is no convergence anywhere. Again, he asked:

Question: Because it obstructs all vows. Answer:
When the six sense faculties are unmoving, no vows arise;

To have [an entry] is movement;

Mastery over knowledge and vision is unstained by the six sense objects; seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing constitute the subsequently attained [wisdom], while prior realization serves as its foundation.
If one does not take realization as primary, nothing will exist.
"Knowing and seeing follow defilement. Question:

With clear knowledge and vision, one attains mastery over realization;

subsequently, for all subsequent attainments (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), the fundamental and the subsequent are clearly distinguished in every instance, liberated in every instance, and practiced in every instance.
When the mind does not arise upon seeing forms with the eyes, this is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
To see with mastery is subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
When the mind does not arise upon hearing sounds with the ears, this is fundamental wisdom.
Mastery over hearing is subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
The non-arising of the mind that perceives odors through the nose is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Mastery over smelling is subsequently attained wisdom.

Mastery over such perception is subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
The self-awakening to the non-arising of body and mind is fundamental wisdom.
Mastery over awakening is subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
The mental cognition that does not give rise to the mind of dharmas is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Mastery over knowledge is subsequently attained wisdom.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
Wisdom devoid of skillful means binds those of the two vehicles.
While in meditative concentration they do not hear [the Dharma], but upon emerging from concentration they do hear it.
Being in concentration without wisdom, they cannot preach the Dharma nor can they deliver sentient beings.
When the mind is scattered upon emerging from meditative absorption, yet is moistened by the water of the Dharma’s concentration, it is called "dry-wisdom concentration" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*).
This is termed "bondage through wisdom lacking skillful means.
This is submerged; [whereas] that which possesses wisdom with skillful means is liberation.
The Bodhisattva knows that the six sense bases are fundamentally unmoving;
whether there is sound or no sound, once the sound has subsided,
they constantly hear and constantly accord with this unmoving cultivation.
By attaining this skillful means and right concentration, one immediately attains parinirvāṇa.
This Great Nirvana is called liberation through the wisdom of skillful means;
it is bondage for those who lack the wisdom of skillful means.
Regarding "liberation through wisdom and skillful means": Question:
Is this cessation a skillful means?
Is immovability a skillful means?
What is it that does not move the mind? Answer:
Attaining the state where the mind dwells in immovability is itself a form of movement.
As the *Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching* says:
All phenomena in the world, whether moving or non-moving, possess the characteristics of formation, decay, and instability.
Joy is movement; fear is the movement of retribution, while non-movement is its cessation.
Having extinguished the six consciousnesses, one realizes the emptiness and stillness of *nirvāṇa*.
Whether there is sound or no sound,
once the sound has subsided and faded away, it is no longer heard.
To be greedily attached to the flavor of dhyāna and fall into the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles is called "bondage through lack of wisdom and skillful means."
This is the liberation through wisdom and skillful means.
The bodhisattva does not crave nirvana,
for they clearly perceive the movement of the mind through hearing, seeing, sensing, and knowing.
This is called liberation through wisdom and skillful means.
What is bondage through wisdom lacking skillful means?
It is when a bodhisattva, with a mind of attachment and views, adorns buddha-fields and brings sentient beings to maturity.
To discipline oneself within the states of emptiness, signlessness,
and wishlessness is called "bondage through wisdom lacking skillful means.
What is meant by "liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means"?
A bodhisattva does not adorn the buddha-fields with a mind of attachment or views;
rather, they discipline themselves within the state of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
This is called liberation through skillful means and wisdom.
Lacking wisdom and skillful means is bondage;
viewing nirvana with craving and viewing the buddha-fields [with attachment] is bondage;
realizing the six sense faculties as the buddha-field is bondage.
Immovability is the adornment.
One realizes the immovability of the six sense faculties and understands that the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion is empty.
To take the realization of emptiness as proof for loathing birth-and-death and dwelling in nirvāṇa is called "bondage through lack of skillful means despite possessing wisdom.
To possess both wisdom and skillful means is liberation.
The Bodhisattva, having already transformed the mind of attachment and views into the love for Nirvana,
takes the purification of the six sense faculties as his buddha-field and immovability as its adornment.
Having realized that the six sense faculties are immovable and that the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion is emptiness,
one perceives emptiness yet does not grasp at emptiness as a realization.
One neither loathes birth-and-death nor dwells in nirvana.
This is called liberation through wisdom and skillful means;
bondage through lack of skillful means despite possessing wisdom.
That is to say, a bodhisattva dwells amidst various afflictions such as greed, hatred, and wrong views.
By planting these seeds, one attains the root;
one realizes the six sense faculties as immovable and understands that the nature of greed, anger, and delusion is emptiness.
Seeing emptiness, they take emptiness as their realization;
weary of birth and death, they dwell in nirvana.
Yet, it is through these afflictions—such as greed, anger, and wrong views—that the Bodhisattva plants the roots of all virtues.
When there is sound or no sound, the sound falls away and is no longer heard.
This "not hearing" is called bondage through wisdom lacking skillful means;
it is liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means.
This means that the bodhisattva, having abandoned all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and wrong views, plants the roots for attaining all virtues;
they realize the six sense faculties are immovable and understand that the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion is empty.
Seeing emptiness, they do not grasp at emptiness as a realization.
They do not loathe birth and death, nor do they dwell in nirvana.
Such a bodhisattva is immediately free from all afflictions, such as greed, hatred, and false views.
They cultivate the roots of all virtues and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Whether there is sound or no sound, as sounds fall away, they constantly hear.
This is called skillful means and liberating wisdom.
Furthermore, one contemplates the body:
the body is not separate from illness.
This disease and this body are neither new nor old;
because they depend on the four great elements of the past, they are not new.
Because the present five aggregates are not [the same as before],
body and mind do not arise; thus,
one severs the causes of outflows (*āsrava*).
One shall attain the fruit of the perfection of nirvāṇa, which is neither cause nor effect.
This is the fundamental source of all Buddhas; it is the place where they vanish within the world, and the mind is that very place.
The five aggregates constitute the world;

Such wisdom is form; such insight is the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. In the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, "Great Vaipulya" is the mind, and "Flower Ornament" is form.
The mind is thus wisdom; form is thus insight.
This is the Wisdom Sutra, the Diamond Sutra; "diamond" (vajra) is the mind.
Vigor is form;
the mind is thus wisdom;
form is thus discernment.
This is the Wisdom Sūtra, the Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma; "this" refers to the wondrous Dharma.
Concentration and wisdom are the wondrous Dharma, while the lotus flower is a metaphor.
There still exist concentration and wisdom;
being unstained by the world within the world,
one clearly understands that concentration and wisdom are themselves the sublime Dharma.
Just as a lotus flower dwells amidst the water yet is not defiled by the water,
so too the sovereign functioning of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is not defiled by the six sense objects.
Just as a lotus flower in full bloom, fragrant and cherished by humans and devas,
is used as a metaphor for this purpose:
to cause those who have not yet attained meditative concentration and wisdom to attain them.
"Opening the gate of expedient means to reveal the mark of reality.
The six sense organs being unmoving and so forth is opening the gate of expedient means;
meditative concentration and wisdom are the mark of reality.

Because it contains the storehouse of concentration and wisdom, the storehouse of all perfected dharmas and characteristics, and the untainted Dharma, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is a treasury that ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles cannot reach.
Neither celestial Māras nor non-Buddhist paths can destroy it;
because it is profound, it is remote and secluded,
such that no one can reach it.
That which cannot be reached by ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles is called "profound.
That which cannot be destroyed by celestial Māras or non-Buddhist paths is called "eternal.
Thus, it is said that when the Bodhisattvas preach the Mahāyāna sūtras, they are called "of immeasurable meaning."
The Dharma taught for Bodhisattvas, protected by the Buddhas’ mindful attention.
Question: Is this the Mahāyāna sūtra?
Is wisdom the Mahāyāna sūtra?
It is also called the Lotus Sutra;
it is the meaning of the "Infinite Meanings" and accords with the principle of the nature of the single true reality.
The teaching of the Bodhisattva-dharma;
the teaching of the Bodhisattva’s methods of concentration and wisdom;
that which is protected by the mindfulness of the Buddha, being originally and inherently free from the need for mindfulness.
Having spoken this sutra, he sat cross-legged to signify the immovability of body and mind; his body was unmoving,
and his physical form was thus [a manifestation of] wisdom.
The mind is unmoving; such is wisdom.
These three are correct clarity.
This is the correct mind.
Practicing in accordance with the principle of the single true reality,
this is called entering the Samādhi of the Place of Immeasurable Meaning;
it signifies that body and mind are unmoving.

"The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable. [Question: What is this?
This cessation and this wisdom are profoundly deep.
The ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is called "profound" because it is bottomless;
it is called "immeasurable" because his insight can transcend the six sense objects.
This gateway of wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter;
it is beyond the comprehension of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The minds of those of the two vehicles give rise to notions of arising and ceasing, and thus they find it difficult to understand.
The minds of śrāvakas possess conceptual grasping and movement, making them difficult to enter from afar;
the bodhisattvas are without grasping and without movement, making it easy for them to understand and enter from afar. Question:
Why is it that the five stages of śrāvakas cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom?
Even if one exhausts all thought and deliberates together with others, one still cannot know it. Question:
Is it because of the object (ālambana) that it is unknown? Answer:
It is because there is a mind seeking [to know] that one cannot know it.
One knows it immediately upon its arising and ceasing;
one knows it through a mind free from seeking. Question:
What is the use of seeking? Answer:
He will transform the thoughts within his mind into wisdom.
Furthermore, he told Śāriputra:

I have now fully attained it;

Those with overweening pride will certainly not respect or believe it upon hearing it.
This is overweening pride (*adhimāna*); it is the state of having nothing to attain.
This superior dharma is increased by the mind that perceives something to be attained.
To be proud toward the superior dharmas of others is overweening pride. Question:
"Is this 'submergence' (maithuna) or is it 'pride' (māna)? Answer:
To deviate from principle is "submergence"; to transgress pride is "pride. Deviation is submergence.
The principle is contrary [to this], for there is no realization of a principle to be attained;
in the higher Dharma there is nothing to be gained,
whereas those of the Two Vehicles increase their gains.
The supreme Dharma has no realization;
the persons of the Two Vehicles increase their realization.
To increase and thereby attain increased realization is to deviate from the principle.
The supreme Dharma is without attainment and without realization; being without attainment and without realization is itself the departure from overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
*Dānapāramitā* is a term in the Sanskrit language.
In this context, "giving" (dāna) is translated as "bestowing.
To give of one's own person while seeing that others do not give is to be arrogant toward the superior dharma of others.
One does not perceive giving,
nor does one perceive non-giving;
these two characteristics are equal.
Pride does not arise;
from this generosity, one attains freedom from overweening pride.
This is called the superior grade of pāramitā.
*Śīlapāramitā* is a Sanskrit term;
in this land, it is translated as "precepts" (*jie*).
One observes the precepts oneself while seeing others breaking them.
This is to be arrogant toward the supreme Dharma;
one does not perceive the two marks of upholding precepts and breaking precepts as being equal.
When pride does not arise, one attains freedom from overweening pride (*adhimāna*) through this precept;
this is called the superior grade of *pāramitā*.
*Kṣānti-pāramitā* is a Sanskrit term.
In this stage, what was previously called "patience" (kṣānti) is now termed "endurance.
One endures within oneself, yet when seeing the anger of others, one gives rise to a sense of superiority toward them;
thus, one does not perceive the existence of patience.
Seeing no anger, these two aspects are equal,
and thus pride does not arise.
From this stage of patience upward, one attains freedom from overweening pride;
this is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). *Vīrya-pāramitā* is a Sanskrit term.
In this context, "going forth" (pravrajyā) is translated as "diligence" (vīrya).
If one is diligent oneself yet sees others as indolent,
this constitutes arrogance toward the superior qualities of others.
One does not perceive diligence,
nor does one perceive indolence;
these two characteristics are equal.
Pride does not arise;
from this point onward, one attains freedom from overweening pride.
This is called the superior grade of pāramitā.
*Dhyānapāramitā* is a term from the Sanskrit language.

In this context, it is translated as "dhyāna-concentration" (*dhyānasamādhi*). When one practices dhyāna-concentration within oneself while observing others' distraction, this constitutes a form of pride regarding superior dharmas in others.
One does not perceive meditative concentration,
nor does one perceive distraction;
these two characteristics are equal.
Pride does not arise;
from this meditative concentration, one attains freedom from overweening pride.
This is called the superior grade of pāramitā.
*Prajñāpāramitā* is a term from the Sanskrit language;
here it is translated as "wisdom.
One perceives that one possesses wisdom within oneself, while perceiving others as ignorant and lacking wisdom.
This is to be arrogant toward the supreme Dharma;
one does not perceive the existence of wisdom,
nor does one perceive the existence of delusion.
When the pride of equanimity toward these two marks does not arise,
one attains freedom from overweening pride (*adhimāna*) through this superior wisdom;
this is called the supreme *prajñāpāramitā*.
To see one's own body as handsome and to see others as ugly and flawed is to be arrogant toward the superior Dharma.
One does not perceive any mark of excellence,
nor does one perceive any mark of ugliness or defilement;
these two characteristics are equal.
Pride does not arise.
From this form, one attains freedom from overweening pride; this is the form of a Buddha.
One perceives that one's own body possesses power.
To see others as lacking power is to be arrogant toward those of superior Dharma;
yet one does not see that they possess power.
Not perceiving any lack of power,
these two aspects are equal,
and thus pride does not arise.
From this power upward, one attains freedom from overweening pride;
this is the power of the Buddha.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world for the sake of the single great cause and condition.
"This cessation is the cause;
this cessation is the condition. Answer:
"To know that [ignorance] is the cause and [views] are the conditions—then these causes and conditions constitute the single great matter of conditions."
Non-perception (*amati*) acts as the causal condition (*nidāna*);
non-seeing (*amadarśana*) acts as the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).
The mind knows by means of the eye’s seeing.
Because of the mind’s cognition, one knows that this is ceasing.
Because of the eye’s seeing, one sees that this is ceasing.

This is the passing away and this is the appearance in the world.
The five aggregates constitute the world;
realizing emptiness is the appearance in the world.
The Tathāgata was born in a royal palace and attained parinirvāṇa between the twin trees;
this is precisely what it means for him to appear in the world.
This appearance refers to the manifestation of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who come to open for sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Question:
Question: Does one hear sounds? Answer:
Hearing hearing becomes submerged;
when the arising of hearing-sounds does not move, [this is true hearing].
Immovability is the opening;
the opening is the gate that reveals the convergence below as awakening.
Uninterrupted cultivation is the entry into this revelation.
It belongs to the Buddha’s realization and to those who practice;
it is opened where there is no going,
and revealed where there is no going.
Ignorance is revealed within the five aggregates;
ignorance is demonstrated within the five aggregates.
The faculty of hearing is form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are merely the mind and the ear-faculty.
When these five aggregates hear a sound without being moved,
one attains the emptiness of the five aggregates.
One attains the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
When a student listens with their faculty of hearing fully attentive,
as soon as a sound occurs, they point to it and their realization becomes distinct.
Entering realization through practice, one takes up the path of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Immovability is the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; the practitioner, with ears alert, listens attentively to this, which is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
There are those who, upon hearing the sound of the teaching, attain clear and distinct realization;
this is the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Having entered into practice through such realization, they take up the path of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
When the Buddha speaks of the *prajñāpāramitā*, it is not actually the *prajñāpāramitā*;
it is merely designated as the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Prajñāpāramitā is that which all Buddhas of the three periods of time have taught in their lands.
Because it is immovable, it is not a ground grasped by worldly people;
therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā is called the "groundless" Prajñāpāramitā.
Non-attachment to signs is wisdom (*jñāna*);
signlessness is insight (*prajñā*).
The Buddha said that the multitude of atoms is not a multitude of atoms; it is merely called a "multitude of atoms."
Because the lands of the Buddhas of the three periods of time are immovable,
they are not what worldly people grasp as a multitude of atoms;
this is called the signless multitude of atoms.
Non-attachment to signs is wisdom (*jñāna*);
signlessness is insight (*prajñā*).
Thus the Buddha said.
The lamp is not a lamp;
it is called a lamp because it is immovable.
This is not the lamp of grasping at signs used by worldly people;
it is called the lamp of signlessness.
Non-grasping at signs is wisdom.
"Signlessness is the second realization of wisdom. Vimalakīrti said:
"O Śāriputra, have you not heard that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess a liberation called 'inconceivable'? [Śāriputra] asked.
"This cessation is beyond thought and deliberation. He replied:
"The mind does not think and the mouth does not deliberate.
When the mind does not think, the mind is free from fetters."
The mind attains liberation;
the mouth does not deliberate upon forms.
Thus, form is free from bondage.
Form attains liberation;
mind and form are both freed from bondage.
This is called inconceivable liberation.
If a bodhisattva dwells in this liberation,
he can place the height and breadth of Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed,
without there being any increase or decrease.
Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, remains as it was originally. Question:
Is this Mount Sumeru submerged within the mustard seed, such that there is no increase or decrease? Answer:
Mount Sumeru is form (*rūpa*).
A mustard seed is also form;
the mind does not contemplate the mind.
Just as Mount Sumeru and a mustard seed are both the same in the nature of form.
The single suchness-characteristic neither increases nor decreases;
the King of Mountains, Sumeru, remains as it was in its original form.
Only those who are ready for deliverance perceive it.
Mount Sumeru enters into a mustard seed without increase or decrease; yet the original characteristics of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, remain as they were. To this, he replied:

There is no increase or decrease;
this is called the original state of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, remaining as it was.

Due to the conditions of conceptual thought, one does not awaken to or know [this];
yet, by practicing the act of "sinking" and "arising," one comes to know it,
and through non-conceptualization, one comes to know it.
This is "disappearance" (mṛta); this is "only those who should be delivered.
Having already transcended the inconceivable through the power of inconceivable mastery, they manifest disappearance and birth;
thus they behold Mount Sumeru entering a mustard seed.
If the mind does not conceptualize, one does not perceive the relative sizes of Mount Sumeru and a mustard seed;
nor does one perceive an entry, nor a non-entry.
One forms such a vision.
This is what is called true seeing.
Where there is no thought, there is no sign;
where there is no sign, there is neither entry nor non-entry.
This is intended to terrify the śrāvakas and eliminate their mental construction (cittamātra).
As long as the śrāvakas have not yet awakened,
they perceive the relative sizes of Mount Sumeru and a mustard seed.
The śrāvakas have already realized this:
seeing that the nature of Mount Sumeru and a mustard seed is empty,
what is there to enter and what is there not to enter?
This is called seeing Mount Sumeru enter into a mustard seed.
This is called the inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation. Question:
Is this the dharma-gate of inconceivable liberation that involves perishing, or is it one that involves abiding?
To give rise to mental deliberation is bondage; one cannot attain liberation thereby.
When mental deliberation does not arise, one is freed from fetters and attains liberation.
Such is the wisdom of a mind that does not deliberate.
Not discussing form with the mouth—such is this wisdom.
This is called the Dharma-gate of inconceivable wisdom and liberation.
Furthermore, one may cause the waters of the four great oceans to enter into a single pore.
It does not disturb the fish, turtles, crocodiles, and other aquatic creatures,
yet the ocean remains as it was in its original state;
the dragons, spirits, and asuras do not perceive or know that they have entered [it].
He does not disturb these sentient beings either.
He manifests passing away and being born within the four great oceans, yet enters into a single pore without disturbing them. Answer:
The great ocean is form (*rūpa*).
The pores are also form;
the mind does not contemplate the mind.
Just as the seawater and the pores are both the suchness of form.
The single suchness-characteristic does not disturb the fish, turtles, crocodiles, and other aquatic species;
yet the fundamental characteristic of that great ocean remains as it was.
This submergence is because its fundamental characteristic remains as it was. Answer: [As stated above].
The waters of the ocean do not diminish, nor do the pores increase;
just as there is no increase or decrease,
this is called the "suchness of original characteristics."
Question: Do the various dragons, spirits, and ghosts undergo death, birth, and dwelling? Answer:
They dwell depending upon the ocean;
because they rely on the *amūta*, they do not perceive or know [these states].
Answer: If one relies on discursive thought, one does not awaken to it nor know it.
By practicing "submergence and arising," one immediately knows it; by being without discursive thought, one immediately knows it.
They do not disturb these sentient beings either;
they share the same mark of suchness as the suchness of sentient beings, which is like the pores of the ocean water,
and likewise they do not disturb these sentient beings.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva dwelling in this inconceivable liberation may take up the three-thousandfold great thousand-world system: greed constitutes its great thousand,
and hatred its middle thousand.
Ignorance is the small chiliocosm.
Because this arises, there is conceptualization;
thus, there are the fetters of greed, hatred, and ignorance that assemble the cycle of birth and death within the six realms of existence.
It would be as if a potter’s wheel were placed in the right palm and thrown across worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
would it sink or would it turn to the right? Answer.
The above constitutes its function.
This inconceivable function severs greed, hatred, and delusion, and transforms one into entry into Suchness,
casting [the self] beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
The sands of the Ganges are afflictions (*kleśa*).
To transcend these afflictions is to cast oneself beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The sentient beings therein do not perceive this, nor do they realize it is as they have already departed.

"This extinction is the fundamental locus. Answer:
"The inconceivable is the fundamental locus;
it does not cause people to have any appearance of coming or going."
Question: Is this the characteristic of passing away and coming back? Answer:
When the mind arises and engages in deliberation, there is the characteristic of coming and going;
when the mind does not arise and engage in deliberation, there is no characteristic of coming and going.
Yet this world remains as it was originally;
its original state remains as it was when it vanished. Answer:
The six [elements] have been thus from the very beginning because their fundamental characteristics are such.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
there may be sentient beings who delight in dwelling long in the world and do not seek deliverance.
The Bodhisattva then expands seven days into one kalpa, causing those sentient beings to perceive it as a single kalpa;
for there may be sentient beings who, not delighting in dwelling for long, are nonetheless capable of being delivered.
The Bodhisattva then transforms one kalpa into seven days so that those sentient beings perceive it as seven days;
yet for ordinary worldlings who delight in long dwelling in the world and desire longevity,
he further expands those seven days into one kalpa.
Those of the two vehicles do not delight in dwelling for long and desire to obtain a short duration;
they take one kalpa to be seven days.
By the power of their mental intention, they can thus manifest the lengthening or shortening of time.
When the mind does not arise, there is no extension or brevity.
Furthermore, for those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings, because there is volition, there is extension and brevity;
for the Bodhisattva, because there is no volition, there is no extension or brevity. [From the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*].
The Bodhisattva Brahmā asked Pramati,
"What is the true nature of all phenomena?
Pramati replied, "The true nature of all phenomena is suchness."
This extinction is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Each of the four great elements and the five aggregates has its own intrinsic nature.

From the place of extinction (*amuta*), [the intrinsic nature arises]. This true nature is the mind and consciousness being profoundly still and pure; this is the true nature. Form conditions the eye-consciousness; [this is the true nature]. Question:
"This is cessation; this is the departure from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The limit of detachment (*vairāgya-koṭi*) extends into the future. [The Master] replied:
"When the ear [and other faculties] do not give rise to sense objects, this is the limit of detachment. The Dharma-upādhyāya explains that all phenomena are the true nature (*dharmatā*)."
Just as when the great flow of water is exhausted, the waves cease.
